paragraphs.text: This is an essay by Gwern about GPT-3, a program OpenAI announced in May 2020. GPT-3 is a neural network, a program built from many simple connected parts that learns from examples. It was trained only to guess the next word of Internet text, using 175 billion adjustable settings, called parameters.

paragraphs.text: The author says GPT-3 matters because it showed meta-learning: learning new tasks from a few examples, without special training. Nobody designed it to do this, and it uses an old, simple design. Its gains from growing bigger also kept following the predicted curves, with no sign of slowing.

Nobody designed it to do this, and it uses an old, simple design.

paragraphs.text: A key idea is the "blessings of scale": bigger networks, trained on more data with more computing, learn better and more generally. Human writing quietly contains logic, cause and effect, and history, so predicting it well forces a model to learn those things. The author argues the final, hardest steps in prediction need the most intelligence.

paragraphs.text: This supports the scaling hypothesis: simply training ever larger networks may make ever smarter behavior appear. The author admits he once doubted this and was wrong. He says the experts who predicted failure were wrong too, and few have admitted it.

fuller.text: This long essay by Gwern looks at GPT-3, a program that predicts text, which OpenAI announced in May 2020. It has 175 billion parameters, the adjustable numbers a neural network learns, making it 117 times bigger than the earlier GPT-2. Gwern uses it to argue for the scaling hypothesis: the idea that simple neural networks get smarter just by being made bigger and given more data and computing power.

sentences.text: This long essay by Gwern looks at GPT-3, a program that predicts text, which OpenAI announced in May 2020.
It has 175 billion parameters, the adjustable numbers a neural network learns, making it 117 times bigger than the earlier GPT-2.
Gwern uses it to argue for the scaling hypothesis: the idea that simple neural networks get smarter just by being made bigger and given more data and computing power.

fuller.text: The piece says this matters because scale may be the secret of AGI, meaning general, human-level AI. Decades ago, Hans Moravec forecast that computing cheap enough for early sub-human systems would arrive in the 2020s, and Gwern says that forecast is holding up.

fuller.text: GPT-3 showed meta-learning: it picked up new tasks, like arithmetic or unscrambling anagrams, from a few examples in its prompt, without special training. Its gains also kept following the predicted curve, with no sign of leveling off. Gwern's tentative explanation is that a big network holds countless small sub-models, and with enough data, memorizing loses out to real, general rules.

fuller.text: Why would predicting the next word teach anything deep? Because human writing quietly encodes logic, cause and effect, and how people think. Easy patterns are learned first, and the last small gains, toward humans' roughly 0.7 bits of error per character, demand real understanding.

fuller.text: Gwern concludes that most AI labs lack the conviction to bet on scaling, and that expert critics have no clear model of how progress happens. An appendix warns that agency, meaning acting toward goals, may emerge in powerful models even without human-made data.

brief.text: GPT-3 was over 100 times bigger than the earlier GPT-2. It could learn new tasks from just a few examples, without special training. Its gains from size had not yet started to level off. The author concludes that much bigger models are possible, but most AI experts doubt this idea.
